summary: Specifies how Label Edge Routers should decide whether to MPLS-encapsulate IPv4 packets that carry header options, since inconsistent behavior existed. It updates RFC 3031 and is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Packets with extra notes in their header were treated differently by different routers. This sets one rule so they act the same.

questions: what is a label edge router
how do mpls routers handle ipv4 options
why do ipv4 options threaten mpls networks
subtitle: Ingress label edge routers must decide on MPLS encapsulation without looking at IPv4 header options.

tldr.problem: Different label edge routers handled IPv4 packets with header options differently. Packets that skipped MPLS encapsulation could be IPv4 routed through the core and expose it to denial-of-service attacks.
tldr.mechanism: An ingress LER must decide whether to push a label stack, and which labels to use, without considering any IPv4 options in the packet. The policy may be configurable but should be on by default.
tldr.outcome: Packets that belong to a prefix-based FEC are MPLS encapsulated even when they carry options. This closes a set of attacks on the MPLS core. The RFC updates RFC 3031.

today: RFC 6178 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2011 that updates RFC 3031. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with IPv4 Options at the MPLS Edge
sections.content:
IPv4 header options enable control functions needed in some situations, such as timestamps, security and special routing. Examples include the Strict and Loose Source Route options, the Record Route option and the Router Alert option. They make the IPv4 header longer than the minimum of 20 octets, so routers often handle them as exceptions. Many routers punt such packets from the fast hardware path to the slow software path, which can cause high CPU use.

In MPLS, an ingress label edge router (LER) encapsulates packets that belong to a prefix-based Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) with a label stack, and label switch routers (LSRs) forward them by label without looking at the IPv4 header. There was no formal standard for what an LER should do with IPv4 packets that carry options, so ingress LERs behaved inconsistently.

If an LER forwards such a packet as plain IPv4, two bad things can follow. A downstream LSR may lack the IPv4 routing information and drop the packet, or it must apply IPv4 forwarding rules and may be exposed to IPv4 attacks. The RFC says it adds details not fully addressed in RFC 3031 and RFC 3032, and updates RFC 3031.
sections.eli5: Some packages carry extra notes that make the post office handle them slowly. Different mail rooms did different things with them, and some sent them down roads that were not guarded.

sections.title: How MPLS Handles Packets and Options
sections.content:
MPLS (RFC 3031) encapsulates packets of a prefix-based FEC with a label stack and switches them along a label switched path (LSP) through label switch routers. Intermediate LSRs do not generally process the IPv4 header, with exceptions such as ICMP processing and LSP ping.

Many MPLS deployments rely on this to give layer 3 transparency, much like ATM switches are transparent at layer 2. Such networks often carry minimal IPv4 routing information in the LSRs, for example no BGP transit routes, because MPLS forwarding of transit packets does not need it. An LER that cannot MPLS encapsulate option packets cannot operate in such environments.
sections.eli5: Inside the post office, workers just follow the tag on the package and never open it. That only works if every package gets a tag at the front desk.

sections.title: The Ingress LER Requirement
sections.content:
An ingress LER MUST implement one policy: when deciding whether to push an MPLS label stack onto an IPv4 packet, it makes the decision without considering any IPv4 options in the header. The label values in the stack are also chosen without considering the options.

The policy MAY be configurable, but it SHOULD be enabled by default. It SHOULD NOT change the handling of signaling messages or data packets that have more specific forwarding rules, such as RSVP (RFC 2205) or source routing (RFC 791). How the LER processes the options before encapsulation is out of scope, since that happens before the packet enters the MPLS domain.

The abstract puts it as: the behavior is mandatory to implement, but optional to invoke.
sections.eli5: The rule is simple. When the front desk decides which tube to put a package in, it ignores any sticky notes on the package.

sections.title: Attacks the Policy Prevents
sections.content:
A router's exception path is often shared with its control and management protocols, so a flood of packets with options can trigger a denial of service (DoS). If option packets in a prefix-based FEC skip MPLS encapsulation at the ingress LER, they are IPv4 routed across the core, and an outside attacker can craft them on purpose. The RFC lists these attacks, assuming downstream LSRs lack protection:

  • Saturating the software forwarding paths of downstream LSRs, which hurts control and management protocols.
  • TTL expiry attacks on core LSRs. MPLS normally hides the core as a single router hop (RFC 3443), but packets that bypass encapsulation lose that hiding, which also exposes network topology.
  • Attacks on LSRs that lack IPv4 routing information, which can trigger ICMP destination unreachable messages.
  • Bypassing LSP Diffserv tunnels (RFC 3270) and the MPLS Class of Service marking policies at the ingress, which could harm high-priority traffic or allow theft of service.
  • Crafted RSVP packets that build RSVP soft state on downstream LSRs, leading to theft of service or exhausted LSR resources.

Packets in a BGP/MPLS IPv4 VPN are always encapsulated at the ingress per RFC 4364, so these VPN services are not subject to the threats above. IPv6 uses extension headers rather than header options, so it is out of scope.
sections.eli5: A sneaky person could put special notes on packages to slip them onto the unguarded road and jam the back rooms of the post office. Ignoring the notes keeps every package on the guarded road.

sections.title: Router Alert Label Imposition
sections.content:
The MPLS Router Alert Label (label value 1, defined in RFC 3032) is analogous to the Router Alert IPv4 option (option value 148). It tells downstream LSRs to look at the MPLS packet more closely, and such packets are also handled as exceptions. At the time of writing, its only legitimate use was LSP ping and trace (RFC 4379).

Since there was no formal standard for Router Alert Label imposition at ingress LERs, an attacker could craft IPv4 packets with options such as Router Alert to force an LER to impose the label and cause a DoS on downstream LSRs. This threat applies to both BGP/MPLS IPv4 VPNs and the plain IPv4 address family. The policy in this RFC prevents such options from forcing imposition of that label.
sections.eli5: There is a special red flag that makes mail workers stop and inspect a package. Attackers could trick the front desk into attaching it, so the front desk now ignores the notes that ask for it.
